title: Κολοιὸς καὶ περιστεραί
part: The Jackdaw and the Doves (Chambry 163 · Perry 129)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 163 (= Perry 129). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κολοιὸς ἰδὼν περιστερὰς ἔν τινι περιστεροτροφείῳ καλῶς τρεφομένας, λευκάνας ἑαυτὸν ἧκεν ὡς καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς διαίτης μεταληψόμενος.
sentences.tr: Koloios idōn peristeras en tini peristerotropheiōi kalōs trephomenas, leukanas heauton hēken hōs kai apo tēs autēs diaitēs metalēpsomenos.
sentences.l: A jackdaw, having seen doves in a dovecote being well fed, having whitened himself, came so as to take a share of the same way of living as well.
sentences.i: A jackdaw saw some doves in a dovecote being well fed, whitened himself, and came to have his share of the same living.
sentences.n: ὡς with a future participle (μεταληψόμενος) gives the purpose as the doer himself conceived it — 'meaning to share'. μεταλαμβάνω takes a genitive of what one gets a portion of, and here ἀπό stands before it, the share reckoned as coming from a source. ἰδών … τρεφομένας is a verb of perceiving with the supplementary participle: he saw them in the act of being fed. δίαιτα again — the way of living is what these jackdaw fables keep returning to.

sentences.t: Αἱ δέ, μέχρι μὲν ἡσύχαζεν, οἰόμεναι περιστερὰν αὐτὸν εἶναι, προσίεντο· ἐπειδὴ δέ ποτε ἐκλαθόμενος ἐφθέγξατο, τηνικαῦτα ἀμφιγνοήσασαι αὐτοῦ τὴν φωνὴν ἐξήλασαν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Hai de, mechri men hēsychazen, oiomenai peristeran auton einai, prosiento· epeidē de pote eklathomenos ephthenxato, tēnikauta amphignoēsasai autou tēn phōnēn exēlasan auton.
sentences.l: And they, so long as he kept quiet, thinking him to be a dove, admitted him; but when at some point, having quite forgotten himself, he gave voice, then, having failed to place his voice, they drove him out.
sentences.i: And so long as he kept quiet they took him for a dove and let him in; but when at last he forgot himself and gave voice, they could not place the sound and drove him out.
sentences.n: ἐκλαθόμενος is 'having quite forgotten' — the compound is stronger than the simple verb, and what he forgets is himself. φθέγγομαι is to utter a sound, of birds as of men. ἀμφιγνοήσασαι is the same verb used of the crows in fable 161, here in the aorist — the moment of failing to place him, not a state of doubt: what defeats both sets of birds is that they cannot make out what they are hearing.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς ἀποτυχὼν τῆς ἐνταῦθα τροφῆς ἐπανῆλθε πάλιν πρὸς τοὺς κολοιούς· κἀκεῖνοι οὐ γνωρίζοντες αὐτὸν διὰ τὸ χρῶμα τῆς μετ’ αὐτῶν διαίτης ἀπεῖρξαν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Kai hos apotychōn tēs entautha trophēs epanēlthe palin pros tous koloious· kakeinoi ou gnōrizontes auton dia to chrōma tēs met’ autōn diaitēs apeirxan auton.
sentences.l: And he, having failed of the food there, went back again to the jackdaws; and they, not recognizing him because of his colour, shut him out from living with them.
sentences.i: And having missed the food there, he went back again to the jackdaws; but they did not know him, because of his colour, and shut him out of their company.
sentences.n: ἀποτυγχάνω, 'to fail of', and ἀπείργω, 'to shut out from', both take the genitive of the thing missed or barred. κἀκεῖνοι is καὶ ἐκεῖνοι run together by crasis. καὶ ὅς opens the sentence in the old demonstrative way, as it did in fable 161.

sentences.t: Οὕτω τε δυοῖν ἐπιθυμήσας οὐδὲ μιᾶς ἔτυχεν.
sentences.tr: Houtō te dyoin epithymēsas oude mias etychen.
sentences.l: And so, having desired two, he got not even one.
sentences.n: δυοῖν is the genitive of the dual, the form Greek keeps for natural pairs; both ἐπιθυμέω and τυγχάνω take the genitive, so the two numbers stand in the same case and the line snaps shut on itself: two wanted, not one had. μιᾶς is feminine, agreeing with διαίτης understood.

sentences.t: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς δεῖ τοῖς ἑαυτῶν ἀρκεῖσθαι, λογιζομένους ὅτι ἡ πλεονεξία πρὸς τῷ μηδὲν ὠφελεῖν πολλάκις καὶ τὰ προσόντα ἀφαιρεῖται,
sentences.tr: Atar oun kai hēmas dei tois heautōn arkeisthai, logizomenous hoti hē pleonexia pros tōi mēden ōphelein pollakis kai ta prosonta aphaireitai,
sentences.l: So then we too must be content with our own, reckoning that greed, besides benefiting us in nothing, often takes away what we already have as well.
sentences.i: So then we too must be content with what is ours, and reckon that greed, over and above doing us no good, will often strip us of what we have besides.
sentences.n: A closing formula that turns on the audience rather than on a third party: Ἀτὰρ οὖν καὶ ἡμᾶς δεῖ, 'so then we too must'. ἀρκέομαι, 'be satisfied with', takes the dative. πρὸς τῷ with the articular infinitive is 'besides, over and above'. τὰ προσόντα is 'the things already belonging to one'. Chambry's page closes this sentence with a comma rather than a full stop; the comma is kept here as printed, and is not a slip in the transcription.
